presentingComplaint: 10 days of stepwise rising fever, headache, and abdominal discomfort
history: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 10-day history of fever that began low-grade and has progressively increased each day in a stepladder pattern, now peaking at 39.8°C in the evenings. She reports frontal headache, malaise, anorexia, and diffuse abdominal discomfort with constipation for the last 4 days (no diarrhea). She denies cough, dysuria, or joint pains. She works at a roadside food stall and admits to frequently eating uncooked salads and drinking water from unfiltered sources; she recalls a similar febrile illness affecting a co-worker two weeks ago. No recent travel outside the city, no tick or animal exposure, no rash noticed by the patient herself. No prior antibiotics in the last 90 days. Not pregnant, no known comorbidities, no immunosuppression.
examination: Toxic-looking but alert and oriented young woman. Temperature 39.7°C with a pulse of 82/min — a pulse-temperature dissociation (relative bradycardia) is noted by the examining team. Blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air. A few faint blanching, salmon-colored macules (rose spots) are seen over the upper abdomen. Abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender with soft hepatosplenomegaly (liver 2 cm, spleen tip palpable). No neck stiffness, no rash elsewhere, chest clear, no murmurs, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.

labs.widalTest: single-sample Widal sent but interpreted with caution due to low specificity

imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: mild hepatosplenomegaly, no free fluid, no focal hepatic lesion, gallbladder wall unremarkable, mesenteric lymph nodes mildly prominent
microbiology: Blood culture (2 sets, drawn prior to antibiotics): growth of Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi at 48 hours, sensitivities pending/reported (guides definitive therapy and fluoroquinolone/azithromycin decision)
Stool culture: sent, may also yield S. Typhi in a minority of cases
Widal serology: single acute sample, low specificity/sensitivity, not diagnostic alone
differentialDiagnoses: Pyrexia of unknown origin, other causes
finalDiagnosis: Enteric fever (typhoid) due to Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, blood culture confirmed
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Salmonellosis (Typhoid and Paratyphoid Fever)
IDSA Guidelines for management of typhoid fever (general reference, no specific year cited)
stewardship: Empirical therapy pending sensitivities: parenteral third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) is favored empirically in areas with fluoroquinolone-resistant/decreased-susceptibility S. Typhi; oral azithromycin is an alternative for uncomplicated cases; fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) may be used only if local susceptibility is confirmed. De-escalate to a susceptibility-directed oral agent once culture results and antibiogram are available, typically completing a 7–14 day course depending on agent and clinical response.
contraindications: Avoid empirical fluoroquinolone monotherapy in regions with high rates of decreased ciprofloxacin susceptibility without confirmed susceptibility
Avoid antipyretics/NSAIDs that mask fever pattern before diagnosis is secure; use paracetamol cautiously given potential hepatic involvement
Avoid unnecessary corticosteroids unless criteria for severe/complicated typhoid (e.g., shock, altered sensorium) are met
edgeCases: Widal test alone is unreliable for diagnosis due to cross-reactivity and prior exposure/vaccination; blood culture remains the diagnostic gold standard
Relative bradycardia may be absent in children and can be masked by concurrent dehydration or fever-associated tachycardia
Intestinal perforation or GI bleeding are feared complications typically occurring in the third week of untreated illness — must monitor for severe abdominal pain, peritonism, or melena
Paratyphoid fever (S. Paratyphi A/B) presents similarly and is not separately listed in the diagnosable disease set; it is captured under the same ENTERIC_FEVER category
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag the classic triad of stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, and rose spots/hepatosplenomegaly as highly suggestive of enteric fever, recommend blood cultures before antibiotics, and note that Widal testing alone is not diagnostic.
expectedNextQuestions: Any travel to or residence in a typhoid-endemic area, or exposure to contaminated food/water?
Any signs of complications — severe abdominal pain, guarding, melena, altered mental status?
